My Farm Advisor · Assignment 2

Three growers, thirty fields, five seasons

A field-level comparison of boundary geometry, the 2019–2023 cropland history, the 2021–2025 growing seasons, and whether that heat supports the county's recommended corn maturity. Static outputs, assembled once.

1What the data says

Five findings survived the checks. One of them is a null result, and it is the most useful of the five.

0.34 vs 0.63 Median compactness, CSB blocks vs OSM parcels. Shape is a provenance story first.
75% corn after corn Nebraska, against 24% in Illinois and 14% in Iowa. Rotation separates the growers.
2,076.3 GDD Nebraska seasonal mean, against 1,841.0 in Illinois and 1,719.2 in Iowa, April–September.
0.7–2.6% Of weather variance sits within a grower-year. Weather cannot rank fields, and the report says so.
4 of 5 seasons Iowa falls short of its county corn-maturity target. Illinois misses 3 of 5, Nebraska 2 of 5.

1.1 Boundary provenance dominates field shape

The two boundary sources produce two populations. CSB fields are large and irregular, with a median compactness of 0.34; OSM parcels are smaller and rounder, at 0.63. Within the CSB population, larger fields are less compact (Spearman -0.588), consistent with long survey-aligned blocks. OSM parcel size shows no such relationship. A farm that mixes sources will always look bimodal, so field size cannot be read as a management choice.

1.2 Rotation is the sharpest between-grower contrast

Nebraska runs continuous corn: 75% of eligible corn field-years follow corn. Illinois and Iowa alternate, at 24% and 14%. The crop-mix association across growers is real but moderate (Cramér's V 0.24), because Illinois and Iowa are more similar to each other than either is to Nebraska. Continuity makes it concrete: 70% of Nebraska fields have held corn for three or more consecutive years, and 50% never left corn in the five-year window.

1.3 Weather is a grower and year covariate — not a field one

Growing-season heat is mostly a grower property: 75.6% of GDD variance sits between growers. Precipitation is mostly year-to-year: 80.7% of its variance sits between years within a grower, with a consistent grower offset. In both cases only 0.7–2.6% of the variance sits within a grower-year, because fields share NASA POWER grid cells. The map in section 5 shows the same thing visually: within a grower the colour barely changes.

Read this as a null result, not a missing analysis. With four, two, and two grid cells across the three growers, field-to-field weather differences measure the grid, not the farm. Ranking fields on weather would be manufacturing a signal.

1.4 The recommended maturity is close, but not met every season

The county maturity product turns a five-year heat total into a relative maturity: RM 100.5 for Iowa, 109.9 for Illinois, and 117.1 for Nebraska. Season by season, and using the same GDD definition the maturity product uses, Iowa runs 57 GDD below its target and misses it in 4 of 5 seasons; Illinois runs 25 GDD below and misses 3; Nebraska runs 7 GDD above and misses 2. The worst single season is Iowa, 108 GDD short in one year — about 5.4 RM of hybrid.

This is a heat test, not a yield test. The county target is a county average, so part of each gap is where the farm sits; what it supports is a decision about moving to an earlier hybrid, and the answer differs by grower. The runtime carries no yield, as-applied, or cost data, so nothing here claims a performance or profit effect.

6Maturity fit and field signals

The county maturity product turns a five-year heat total into a relative maturity. Tested against each season, that recommendation is met in some years and missed in others — and the shortfall is a hybrid decision, not a yield claim. The runtime carries no yield, cost, or profit data.

Maturity fit compares whole-calendar-year GDD with a 30 °C cap against the county RM requirement, a different definition from A3. The county target is built from the county weather table, so a level offset is location. Wilson intervals cover the two proportions; n is five seasons or ten fields per grower.

7Limits and caveats

  • Weather is gridded. NASA POWER resolves to IA 2, IL 4, NE 2 for the three growers. Within-grower field comparison is therefore a grid comparison, reported as a null result.
  • CDL is a 30 m raster. The smallest field-year in this run has 4 pixels (a 1.3 ha parcel), so crop shares are quantised. Partial coverage can push a field's percentages below 100.
  • Source and size are confounded. CSB fields are both larger and less compact. The analysis reports the within-source correlation alongside the between-source comparison rather than attributing the effect to one.
  • Small n. Thirty fields and fifteen grower-years support effect sizes and intervals, not population claims about “growers” in general.
  • Maturity fit is not yield. The county RM target is a county-average planning value built from the county weather table, not from these ten fields, so a level offset is location rather than management. A shortfall says the recommended maturity is late for that heat; it says nothing about how the hybrid actually yielded.
  • Two GDD definitions. Seasonal figures use April–September with no cap; maturity fit uses the whole calendar year capped at 30 °C, matching the county maturity product. Subtracting one from the other would invent a shortfall.
  • No yield, as-applied, or economics data exists in this runtime. Every signal here is a proxy built from rotation, weather, and geometry. The report does not claim crop performance, cost, or profit.
  • Five CDL years only, 2019–2023. That is the pipeline's pinned CDL window, not a gap in the analysis: the program's external-data rule requires sources public by 1 February 2026, and data-pipeline/src/scripts/ingest/download_cdl.py pins DEFAULT_CDL_LATEST_YEAR = 2023 to stay inside it. No 2024–2025, so no completed rotation cycle is guaranteed and the pipeline's predicted next crop cannot be tested here.

8Sources and provenance

Field polygons (OSM subset)OpenStreetMap via Overpass. ODbL 1.0; attribution retained.
Field polygons (CSB subset)USDA NASS Crop Sequence Boundaries via FIBOA GeoParquet. CC-BY-4.0 / USDA public.
Crop historyUSDA NASS Cropland Data Layer, 2019–2023. USDA public data.
WeatherNASA POWER daily data, 2021–2025, April–September for seasonal figures and the full year for maturity fit. Public; gridded, not on-farm measurement.
County maturityCorn RM and soybean MG by FIPS from strategy/maturity-by-fips, derived from the same NASA POWER data. Heuristic planning values, not seed recommendations.
AnalysisOriginal code in my-farm-advisor/eda/field-eda. This report is a one-time artifact outside that subskill.
